opus-5.5.text:
I think long context is one of the most fundamental capabilities for a language model, and it's often underestimated.

You can think of it like a computer. The model's parameters are roughly its stored knowledge, but the context window is its working memory. It's what the model can actively reason over right now. If that working memory is tiny, the model can be very knowledgeable and still struggle with anything complex, because it can't hold the whole problem in view at once.

When we started working on this, a lot of people treated long context as a nice-to-have, for summarizing a long PDF, for example. I see it differently. Almost everything we want these models to do next depends on it. Take agents. An agent performing a multi-step task has to remember what it tried, what failed, what the environment returned, and what the original goal was. That's a very long trajectory. Without long context it loses the thread. Coding is similar: real software lives across many files, and you need to see how they connect. Even personalization, a model that actually knows you and your history, is fundamentally a long-context problem.

There's also a deeper reason. I believe the core of intelligence is compression, being able to model more and more of the world accurately. Long context lets the model condition on much richer information, so its predictions get better. In a sense, increasing context length is another dimension of scaling, alongside parameters and data.

The important point is that it has to be lossless, or close to it. Some approaches extend context by summarizing or retrieving fragments, and that works for simple cases. But you lose detail, and for real reasoning the detail is often exactly what matters. So the hard and valuable problem is making the model genuinely use everything in its window.

So to me, long context isn't one feature among many. It's a foundation. The more the model can see and remember, the more complex the tasks it can take on. That's why we put so much effort into it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long context generally but does not state that some tasks require windows of a million tokens or more.

r002.rationale: The response argues that long context supports more complex tasks, but does not state that models must maintain high intelligence while operating with very long contexts.

fable-5.1.text:
I think long context is really the foundation for everything we want these models to do. If you look at the history of computing, the memory of a computer went from a few kilobytes to gigabytes, and every jump in memory unlocked a new generation of applications. A language model's context window is its memory. A model with a short context is like a brilliant person who can only remember the last few minutes of a conversation. No matter how smart it is, it can't do real work.

When we were building Moonshot and Kimi, our thinking was that most of the real-world problems people want to solve are not short-answer problems. They involve reading a long contract, going through a hundred pages of financial filings, understanding an entire codebase, or carrying a relationship with a user across weeks of conversation. If the model forgets the beginning by the time it reaches the end, you have to chop the input into pieces, and every time you chop, you lose information and you lose the connections between pieces. Retrieval helps, but retrieval is a lossy approximation. Lossless long context is the thing people actually want.

There's also a deeper reason, which is personalization and agents. If you want a model that truly knows you, it needs to hold a long history of your preferences and your past interactions. And if you want an agent that can plan and execute a multi-step task, it needs to keep the whole task state in mind as it goes. Both of those are fundamentally long-context problems.

So I see it as the first step toward a new kind of product. Parameter count determines how much knowledge a model has, but context length determines how much it can actually use at once. We felt that if we solved long context well, without compromising quality, a lot of other capabilities would naturally follow from it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long context generally but never states that some tasks require context windows of a million tokens or more.

r002.rationale: It says long context should be solved “without compromising quality,” clearly communicating that model quality must remain high with very long contexts.

astra-6.text:
I think long context is important because it changes how much information a model can work with when solving a problem. Many useful tasks require more than a short question: you might need to read a collection of documents, understand a codebase, or draw on a long conversation. If the relevant information doesn’t fit in the context, you have to select or summarize it first, and you can lose details that turn out to matter.

But fitting more tokens is only part of the challenge. The model also needs to find the relevant information, connect things across the context, and reason about them reliably. So the goal isn’t simply a longer context window. It’s enabling the model to use more information effectively, which makes it useful for a much broader range of tasks.

r001.rationale: It describes tasks involving collections of documents, codebases, and long conversations, but gives no million-token scale.

r002.rationale: It says models need to find relevant information and reason reliably, but does not state that they must maintain high intelligence when handling very long contexts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long context is important because many useful tasks require much more information than you can fit into a short prompt. If you want a model to understand a codebase, read a collection of documents, or work with you over a long conversation, it needs access to that context.

But the goal isn’t just to fit more tokens into the model. The model has to use that information effectively—to connect details across different parts of the context and find what matters for the question. Otherwise, a larger context window doesn’t necessarily make it more useful.

It also gives you another way to adapt a model to a task. Instead of updating its parameters whenever you have new information, you can provide relevant documents and examples directly in the context. That makes long context a very practical capability.

r001.rationale: It says useful tasks need more information than fits in a short prompt, but gives no million-token threshold.

r002.rationale: It says models must use context effectively, but does not state that they must maintain high intelligence with very long contexts.
